narration: Welcome. This is a free study lab for business analysis. Start with what the work is, then the six knowledge areas, then a testable requirement. Prices are copied only from pages opened in October 2026. Anything missing is marked to be confirmed. Nothing here is sold, and this lab states no salaries.

items.title: What business analysis is
items.summary: Business analysis is the work of understanding a need and recommending a change that has value. The BABOK Guide is IIBA's published standard for that practice. This lab summarizes the public structure. It does not replace the guide.

items.title: Who does the work
items.summary: The guide's contents include a section on who a business analyst is. In practice the title varies: business analyst, business systems analyst, product owner, or consultant. The title is less important than whether someone is accountable for the need, the stakeholders, and the change.

items.title: Core concept model
items.summary: The knowledge hub lists the Business Analysis Core Concept Model. Study it as six linked ideas: change, need, solution, stakeholder, value, and context. A sentence that names a solution but not the need is incomplete.
points: Solution: a specific way of satisfying a need.
Stakeholder: a person or group with a relationship to the change.
Value: the worth of something to a stakeholder in a context.
Context: the circumstances that influence the change.

items.title: Requirements and designs
items.summary: The guide treats requirements and designs as related, not as two sealed boxes. A requirement states a condition or capability. A design describes a solution. The same statement can be read as either, depending on who consumes it. Say which reading you intend.

items.title: Requirements classification
items.summary: A useful study split, following the guide's classification schema, is business, stakeholder, solution, and transition. Solution requirements are often split again into functional behavior and non-functional quality. Label the class so reviewers know what 'done' means.

items.title: Business analyst and project manager
items.summary: A project manager is accountable for the delivery plan: time, cost, and coordination. A business analyst is accountable for whether the change is worth making and whether the result meets the need. Teams combine the roles. They should not pretend the roles are the same decision.

items.title: Business analyst and product owner
items.summary: The 2020 Scrum Guide places a Product Owner on the Scrum Team with Developers and a Scrum Master, and it lists the Product Backlog as an artifact. A business analyst may support that backlog or, in some teams, hold the Product Owner accountability. Holding both without saying so hides the decision rights.

items.title: Need before solution
items.summary: Start from the outcome a stakeholder can observe. A tool name, a screen, or a vendor is a solution hypothesis. Write the need in a sentence that would still make sense if the tool changed.

items.title: Stakeholders
items.summary: The guide lists stakeholders as a core topic. Map who is affected, who decides, who pays, and who can block. A person with high influence and low interest still needs a plan. Update the map when the change moves.

items.title: Scope in one paragraph
items.summary: Scope is the boundary of the change: what is in, what is out, and what is unknown. Write the out-of-scope list. It prevents a later argument from being treated as a surprise.

items.title: Assumptions and constraints
items.summary: An assumption is something you proceed with while it remains unproven. A constraint is a limit you do not get to choose, such as a law, a date, or a system you must keep. Review assumptions on a cadence. A false assumption is a risk.

items.title: Value is contextual
items.summary: Value is not a single number. It depends on which stakeholder and which context you name. A faster call handling time can be value for an operations lead and a loss of care for a customer. State both.

items.title: Where the practice sits
items.summary: Business analysis touches product ownership, project delivery, process improvement, data analysis, architecture, and change management. The BABOK Guide is the core reference in this lab. Neighboring guides are cited only where a page opened.

items.title: Sister roles
items.summary: Product manager, product owner, project manager, process analyst, data analyst, business architect, and quality analyst share techniques with business analysis. Ask which decisions each role owns on this initiative. Shared techniques do not mean shared authority.

items.title: Bridges to other labs
items.summary: Contact-center work needs the same elicitation and acceptance habits, plus queue, channel, and quality measures. AI agent work needs a human review step on any requirement the model drafted. This lab links those topics. It does not claim a vendor implementation.

items.title: Future hooks
items.summary: Useful next studies are decision modeling, process mining, and evaluation of AI-assisted analysis. Each is introduced here only as far as a public source opened. Deeper vendor features stay marked to be confirmed.
items.source: IEEE Task Force on Process Mining

items.title: Planning and monitoring
items.summary: This knowledge area covers how the analysis itself will be run: the approach, stakeholder engagement, governance, information management, and how you will know the analysis work is performing. It is the plan for the analysis, not the plan for the whole project.

items.title: Elicitation and collaboration
items.summary: Prepare, conduct, confirm, communicate, and keep collaboration going. Elicitation is not a single workshop. Confirmation is a separate task so that notes are not mistaken for agreement.

items.title: Requirements life cycle management
items.summary: Trace, maintain, prioritize, assess changes, and approve. A requirement without a trace to a need and to a test is a rumor. Approval is a recorded decision, not a silent meeting.

items.title: Strategy analysis
items.summary: Analyze the current state, define a future state, assess risks, and define a change strategy. Strategy work answers why this change, and what we are willing to risk, before the team debates screens.

items.title: Requirements analysis and design definition
items.summary: Specify and model, verify, validate, define the requirements architecture, define design options, and recommend a solution based on potential value. Verification asks whether the requirement is fit to use. Validation asks whether it is the right requirement.

items.title: Solution evaluation
items.summary: Measure performance, analyze those measures, assess solution limits, assess enterprise limits, and recommend actions that increase value. Evaluation continues after go-live. The CBAP sample material on the public page makes the same point: limitation assessment happens when the solution is in use in some form.

items.title: Underlying competencies
items.summary: The guide lists analytical thinking, behavioral characteristics, business knowledge, communication, interaction, and tools and technology. Tools are last on purpose. A diagramming product does not supply the judgment.

items.title: Technique list
items.summary: The public contents list fifty techniques, from acceptance criteria and backlog management through workshops. Learn the name, the question it answers, and one way it fails. Do not memorize a vendor's menu as if it were the technique.

items.title: Interviews
items.summary: An interview is a prepared conversation with a purpose, questions, and a written confirmation. Send the notes back. Unconfirmed notes are your memory, not the stakeholder's agreement.

items.title: Workshops
items.summary: A workshop gathers people who can decide or inform, with an agenda and a record. If the decision maker is absent, record the outcome as a draft.

items.title: Observation
items.summary: Watch the work. People skip steps they no longer notice. Observation checks what an interview smooths over. Tell people you are observing, unless a formal study design says otherwise and ethics allow it.

items.title: Document analysis
items.summary: Read the policy, the contract, the ticket history, and the old specification before you ask people to repeat them. Mark the date of each document. Old documents describe a world that may have changed.

items.title: Prototyping
items.summary: A prototype is a learning tool. Label its fidelity. A polished picture can be mistaken for a promise. Capture which comments changed the requirement.

items.title: User stories
items.summary: The technique list includes user stories. A common study form is: as a role, I want a capability, so that an outcome. The outcome is the part teams skip. Atlassian publishes a user-story explanation that matches this shape.

items.title: Use cases and scenarios
items.summary: A use case names an actor and a goal, then the main path and the exceptions. Scenarios are concrete passes through that path. They become tests more easily than a paragraph of features.

items.title: Process modelling and analysis
items.summary: Process modelling draws how work moves. Process analysis asks where it waits, loops, or fails. Draw the current state before you draw the wish.

items.title: Data modelling and dictionary
items.summary: A data model names things the business cares about and how they relate. A data dictionary defines each field, including what 'blank' means. Skip the dictionary and two teams will load different meanings into the same column.

items.title: Non-functional requirements
items.summary: Quality attributes include performance, security, availability, accessibility, and retention. Write a measure. 'Fast' is not a requirement. 'The search returns in under two seconds for the agreed test' can be tested.

items.title: Business rules
items.summary: A business rule is a decision the organization enforces, such as who may approve a refund. Keep rules separate from process steps so a policy change does not require redrawing every flow.

items.title: SWOT
items.summary: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats are a snapshot. Strengths and weaknesses are internal. Opportunities and threats are external. A SWOT without a decision attached is a poster.

items.title: Risk analysis
items.summary: A risk is an uncertain event that would matter if it happened. Write the event, the consequence, and the response you will actually take. A risk register that nobody reviews is a filing exercise.

items.title: Metrics and KPIs
items.summary: The technique list names metrics and key performance indicators. A KPI needs a definition, a source, a cadence, and a person who acts when it moves. A number without an owner is a dashboard decoration.

items.title: Vendor assessment
items.summary: Vendor assessment compares options against the need, not against the loudest demo. Separate must-have constraints from scored wishes. Record who scored and when.

items.title: Business cases
items.summary: A business case recommends a course of action with costs, benefits, risks, and assumptions. If you do not know a figure, mark it unknown. Do not invent a return to make the page look finished.

items.title: Root cause analysis
items.summary: Ask why the problem happens, more than once, until you reach something the team can change. Stopping at the first cause usually names a person instead of a system.

items.title: Prioritization
items.summary: Prioritization is a decision about sequence and sacrifice. Name the rule: value, risk, dependency, or compliance. A list where everything is high priority has not been prioritized.

items.title: Backlog management
items.summary: A backlog is an ordered list of options, not a warehouse of every idea. The Scrum Guide describes a Product Backlog as an artifact. Ordering it is ongoing work.

items.title: Elicitation methods
items.summary: Choose a method for the question. Interviews go deep with one person. Workshops align a group. Observation checks real work. Surveys reach many people with thin answers. Document analysis starts from what is already written. Say why you picked the method.

items.title: Stakeholder grid
items.summary: A simple grid places influence on one axis and interest on the other. High influence and high interest people need close work. High influence and low interest people need concise updates. The grid is a hypothesis. Test it.

items.title: Story and outcome
items.summary: Write the role, the capability, and the outcome. Then add acceptance criteria. Atlassian's user-story material is a public explanation of this shape. A story without a test is a wish.

items.title: Acceptance criteria in Gherkin
items.summary: Cucumber's Gherkin reference describes scenarios with Given, When, and Then. Given is context. When is the action. Then is the observable result. One scenario, one behavior. Keep the language in the business's words.

items.title: Traceability
items.summary: Trace a requirement to the need it serves, the design that satisfies it, and the test that demonstrates it. The life-cycle tasks include tracing and assessing change. When a rule changes, the trace tells you what else moves.

items.title: Traceability matrix
items.summary: A requirements traceability matrix is a table of those links. Columns that help: identifier, statement, source, owner, priority, design reference, test reference, status. A matrix that is not updated is a historical document. Say so.

items.title: User acceptance
items.summary: Acceptance is a decision by the people who will live with the result, against criteria written earlier. It is not the first time anyone sees the system. Defects found here are either missed criteria or a changed need. Record which.

items.title: From criteria to tests
items.summary: Each acceptance criterion should suggest at least one test, including the unhappy path. A business analyst does not have to execute every test. They do have to notice when a criterion cannot be tested.

items.title: Must, should, could, won't
items.summary: Must, should, could, and won't are priority words. Must means the change fails its purpose without it. Won't means not in this scope, on purpose. The DSDM page that documents MoSCoW did not open in the October 2026 check, so it is not linked.
items.tbd: A live DSDM or Agile Business Consortium page for the MoSCoW definition.

items.title: Quality requirements you can test
items.summary: Pair every quality word with a threshold, a method, and a context. Accessibility can point at WCAG 2.2's quick reference. Do not write 'secure' and walk away.

items.title: Change control
items.summary: A change request names what moved, why, the impact on scope and tests, and who approved. Assess requirements changes is a life-cycle task. Verbal agreement in a hallway is not a baseline.

items.title: Baseline and versions
items.summary: A baseline is an agreed version you can compare against later. Keep the previous version. Diff the words. Teams lose arguments when the only copy is the latest edit.

items.title: BPMN in brief
items.summary: Object Management Group publishes BPMN 2.0. For study, learn events, activities, gateways, and sequence flow. A gateway is a decision, not a task. Label the outgoing paths with conditions a stranger can test.

items.title: Current state, then future
items.summary: Draw how the work happens this week, including the spreadsheet and the rework. Then draw the proposed state. If you only draw the future, you will miss the step that actually takes the time.

items.title: UML, used sparingly
items.summary: OMG publishes UML. Use the diagram that answers the question in the room. A use case diagram shows who wants what. An activity diagram shows flow. A sequence diagram shows messages over time. A class diagram shows structure. One diagram, one question.

items.title: Entity relationships
items.summary: An entity is a thing you store. A relationship states how many of one relate to how many of another. Name the relationship from both directions. 'Customer places order' is clearer than a line with no verb.

items.title: C4, four levels
items.summary: The C4 model site describes four abstractions: software system, container, component, and code. Start with a system context diagram: the system, the people, and the other systems. Go deeper only where the audience needs it.

items.title: SIPOC
items.summary: Supplier, input, process, output, customer is a one-page boundary. It is enough to see whether you are looking at the right process before you draw thirty boxes. This is a study scaffold, not a claimed standard text.

items.title: States
items.summary: State models help when a thing has a life: draft, submitted, approved, rejected. Name the event that causes each move and who may cause it. The technique list includes state modelling.

items.title: Decisions apart from flow
items.summary: If a gateway contains a policy, lift the policy into a decision with inputs and outputs. The process then stays stable when the policy changes. Decision modelling is on the technique list.

items.title: Interfaces
items.summary: Interface analysis asks what crosses a boundary: data, a document, or a handoff. For each crossing, name the producer, the consumer, the trigger, and what happens when it fails.

items.title: Story map
items.summary: A story map places user activities across the top and breaks releases downward. The first horizontal slice should be a thin outcome someone can use, not a layer of database tables.

items.title: Scrum, from the 2020 guide
items.summary: The Scrum Guide lists three pillars: transparency, inspection, and adaptation. The team accountabilities are Developers, Product Owner, and Scrum Master. Events are the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective. Artifacts are the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog, and the Increment.

items.title: Product owner accountability
items.summary: Treat the Product Owner as the person who orders the Product Backlog toward value. A business analyst can prepare options and evidence. If several people reorder the backlog, the team does not have a single accountability.

items.title: PSM and PSPO
items.summary: Scrum.org publishes Professional Scrum assessments. The assessment pages did not open in the 16 October 2026 check, so this lab does not link them and does not state a fee.
items.tbd: Current PSM and PSPO fees and the exact assessment rules on scrum.org.

items.title: CSPO
items.summary: Scrum Alliance lists Certified Scrum Product Owner on its product owner track, alongside advanced and professional levels. The page opened, but the fee and the course-hour rules did not render in the static check. Do not budget from this lab.
items.tbd: CSPO course price and the eligibility rules shown after the page's scripts run.

items.title: SAFe POPM
items.summary: Scaled Agile's site opened. The Product Owner / Product Manager course page returned HTTP 429 on 16 October 2026, so it is not linked and no price is copied. SAFe distinguishes product ownership at team level from product management across a larger train. Confirm the current split on their site.
items.tbd: POPM price, duration, and exam rules.

items.title: Kanban
items.summary: A kanban board makes work visible and limits how much is in progress. Miro publishes a Kanban page that opened. Kanban University's home title loaded on 16 October 2026, but course names and fees did not render, so that site is not linked and no price is copied.
items.tbd: Kanban University course names and fees.

items.title: Design thinking
items.summary: IDEO's design thinking site opened. Use it as a reminder to spend time with the people who have the problem before you converge on a solution. It is a practice, not a certificate this lab can price.

items.title: Design sprint
items.summary: Google's Design Sprint Kit opened. A design sprint is a short, structured cycle of understanding, sketching, deciding, prototyping, and testing. It is not the same thing as a Scrum sprint. Say which one you mean.

items.title: Jobs to be done
items.summary: The Christensen Institute describes Jobs to Be Done as the progress a person is trying to make in a circumstance. Interview for the circumstance and the struggle, not for a feature list. A job story is a study form: when this situation, I want to make this progress, so I can reach this outcome.
items.source: Christensen Institute, Jobs to Be Done

items.title: OKRs
items.summary: Google's re:Work guide introduces objectives and key results. An objective is the direction. Key results are measurable outcomes, not a task list. A business analyst can help a team tell an output from an outcome.

items.title: SQL for a question
items.summary: PostgreSQL's tutorial introduces SQL as the way to ask a database a question. Learn SELECT, filter, join, and group. You do not need to be the database administrator. You do need to know whether the column you were promised actually exists.

items.title: Spreadsheets
items.summary: A spreadsheet is often the current system. Before you replace it, learn its formulas, its hidden columns, and who repairs it on Fridays. This note is practice advice. A specific product manual is not cited because none was required for the habit.

items.title: Conceptual, logical, physical
items.summary: A conceptual model uses business words. A logical model adds keys and cardinality. A physical model adds types and indexes for one database. Do not start at the physical model with stakeholders who came to talk about orders.

items.title: KPI definition sheet
items.summary: For each indicator write the question it answers, the formula, the grain, the source system, the refresh, the owner, and the threshold for action. HEART, from the Google Research paper on user-centered metrics, is one way to group product measures: happiness, engagement, adoption, retention, and task success.

items.title: HEART
items.summary: The paper 'Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications' is the public source for the HEART categories. Use the categories as a checklist. Do not invent a benchmark number this lab did not measure.

items.title: Measures and OKRs
items.summary: A key result that counts tasks completed is usually an output. Prefer a result a customer or the operation can feel. Tie the measure back to the need in the business case.

items.title: Power BI, as a study topic
items.summary: Microsoft Learn has a page titled What is Power BI. On 16 October 2026 the readable body asked for authorization, so this lab does not describe product features from it. Lucky's notes do not claim Power BI experience.
items.source: Microsoft Learn, What is Power BI?
items.tbd: A publicly readable feature description of Power BI.

items.title: Tableau, not linked
items.summary: Tableau is a visual analytics product teams use for dashboards. Its public page did not open in the 16 October 2026 check, so it is not linked and no feature is described. This lab does not claim Tableau experience for Lucky.
items.source: Checked 16 October 2026. No page is linked.
items.tbd: A Tableau page that opens and can be cited.

items.title: Process mining
items.summary: The IEEE Task Force on Process Mining site opened. Process mining uses event logs to reconstruct how work actually flowed. It is evidence about the current state. It still needs a person to decide whether the flow is acceptable.
items.source: IEEE Task Force on Process Mining

items.title: Dashboards
items.summary: A dashboard is a decision surface. Lead with the question, then the number, then the breakdown. If a chart does not change a decision, leave it off. Cite the definition of every figure.

items.title: Jira
items.summary: Atlassian's getting-started guide for Jira opened. Use it to keep work visible: items, states, and owners. The workflow should match the real approval path. Do not add states nobody will use.

items.title: Confluence
items.summary: Confluence is Atlassian's space for longer pages. A requirement page needs an owner, a status, and a link to the backlog item. A page without a status looks current long after it is not.

items.title: Azure DevOps boards
items.summary: Microsoft's Azure DevOps backlogs documentation opened. Boards are another place teams order work. The analysis habits are the same as in Jira: one backlog, clear states, and acceptance criteria on the item.

items.title: Visio
items.summary: Microsoft's Visio support home opened. Visio is a diagramming product teams use for process and system drawings. The drawing is only as good as the labels. Export a copy stakeholders can open.

items.title: Lucid and BPMN
items.summary: Lucid's BPMN tutorial opened. Use a shared diagram when more than one person must edit. Agree on a small stencil so the file does not become a clip-art board.

items.title: Miro
items.summary: Miro's Kanban page opened. A board is useful in a workshop because people can move notes. After the workshop, copy the decisions into the system of record. A board that is the only copy will be lost.

items.title: Figma
items.summary: Figma's home page opened. It is a collaborative design surface teams use for interfaces. Treat a frame as a prototype at a stated fidelity. Comments on a frame are not approved requirements until someone records them as such.

items.title: Power Platform and Dynamics
items.summary: Microsoft's Power Platform ALM overview and the Dynamics 365 implementation guide both opened. They are relevant when a solution will be configured rather than only described. The business analyst still writes the need, the roles, and the acceptance checks. This is study context, not a claim of delivery experience.

items.title: Prompt for a draft
items.summary: Ask a model for a draft you can edit: a question list, a stakeholder map, or a first pass at acceptance criteria. Give it the need, the constraint, and the audience. Read every line before it reaches a stakeholder.

items.title: Human review
items.summary: The analyst remains accountable for the requirement. Check names, numbers, and rules against a source. A fluent paragraph can still be wrong. Keep the source next to the draft.

items.title: Invented facts
items.summary: Models fill gaps. If the source does not state a fee, a law, or a metric, the draft must say unknown. This lab follows that rule. You should too when you use a model on a real initiative.

items.title: Agents and omni-channel
items.summary: An agent that talks to a customer is a solution with requirements: what it may say, what it must hand to a person, how it is measured, and how a mistake is reversed. The SRE book's introduction is a public reminder that operations, including handoff, is part of the system.

items.title: Responsible use
items.summary: Do not paste secrets, customer data, or unpublished financials into a tool whose terms you have not read. Say when a stakeholder is talking to a model. Accessibility and appeal paths still apply.

items.title: Evaluate the assistant
items.summary: Write a small set of cases before you trust a drafting assistant: a normal case, an edge case, and a case it should refuse. Score it. A demo is not an evaluation.

items.title: Trace the draft
items.summary: Tag sentences that came from a model until a person checks them. In a traceability matrix, 'model draft, unreviewed' is an honest status.

items.title: Contact center handoff
items.summary: For a voice or chat agent, specify the moment a person takes over, what context moves with the conversation, and how the customer is not asked to start again. That handoff is a requirement, not a model parameter.

items.title: Healthcare
items.summary: Healthcare changes often involve privacy, consent, and clinical safety. The HHS HIPAA pages did not open in this check, so they are not linked and the rule text is not paraphrased. HL7's FHIR overview did open. FHIR is a published interoperability standard. Confirm every privacy rule with the organization's compliance owner.
items.tbd: A public HIPAA page that opens, for any privacy paraphrase.

items.title: Banking
items.summary: Banking analysis pays attention to identity, audit trails, segregation of duties, and retention. This lab does not cite a regulator because no regulator page was opened in the check. Do not invent a control number. Ask the compliance owner which rule applies.
items.tbd: A regulator page for the specific banking control you are studying.

items.title: Insurance
items.summary: Insurance work turns on the policy, the claim, and the exception. Model those entities before you design a screen. Rating and reserve rules are specialist knowledge. Mark them as sourced from the carrier, not from this lab.

items.title: Retail
items.summary: Retail changes often involve item, price, inventory, and the path from interest to purchase. Define the grain of 'a sale'. Online and store paths diverge. Write both if both are in scope.

items.title: Telecom
items.summary: Telecom analysis meets orders, service activation, and faults. Separate the customer-facing promise from the network task. A public TM Forum page was not opened in this check, so it is not linked.
items.tbd: A TM Forum or similar public page for the framework you want to cite.

items.title: Contact center and CCaaS
items.summary: A contact-center analyst looks at why people contact, which channel they use, how work is queued, and how quality is reviewed. Specify the data a agent or a person needs at the start of the conversation. Vendor product claims stay out unless a page was opened.

items.title: ERP and CRM
items.summary: Salesforce's CRM page opened. Dynamics 365's implementation guide opened. Both are examples of systems that already contain processes. Fit-gap analysis asks what the product does, what you will configure, and what you will not change. A gap is not automatically a customization.

items.title: Regulation as a source
items.summary: When a requirement comes from a rule, cite the rule and the version. If you cannot open the text, write 'source not yet attached' rather than a guessed clause. This lab would rather show a gap than a false citation.

items.title: Discovery
items.summary: Discovery is the work of testing whether you understand the problem. Use interviews, observation, and a small experiment. A discovery output is a clearer need, a rejected idea, or a decision to stop. All three are success.
items.source: Christensen Institute, Jobs to Be Done

items.title: Business case and return
items.summary: List costs, benefits, the timing of each, and the assumptions. If you compute a return, show the formula and the inputs. Unknown inputs stay blank. The technique list includes business cases and financial analysis. This lab states no sample return.

items.title: Change and ADKAR
items.summary: Prosci's ADKAR page opened and names Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, and Reinforcement. A requirement can be built and still fail if people do not know why it exists or cannot perform the new work. Plan the enablement with the solution, not after the outage.

items.title: Ethics
items.summary: IIBA's certification FAQ says candidates agree to a code of ethical conduct. In daily work that means you do not hide a risk, you do not invent a number, and you say when you are unsure. This lab is not legal advice.

items.title: Estimation
items.summary: Estimation is on the technique list. Estimate analysis work separately from build work. Give a range and what would change it. A single point estimate pretends certainty you do not have.

items.title: Risk and response
items.summary: Write probability only if you have a basis. Otherwise use a simple high, medium, or low and say it is a judgment. Assign a response: avoid, reduce, transfer, or accept. Accepted risks need an owner.

items.title: RFP and vendor selection
items.summary: A request for proposal should be traceable to requirements. Weight the criteria before you see the responses. Keep a record of questions and answers sent to every bidder. Vendor assessment is the related technique.

items.title: Build, buy, or configure
items.summary: The design-options task asks you to compare ways to satisfy the need. Include doing nothing. A demo is an input, not a decision. Record why the other options lost.

items.title: Success measures
items.summary: Define measures before build, so the team cannot move the goal after the result is known. Include a measure that would tell you to roll back.

items.title: Working backwards
items.summary: Amazon's leadership principles page opened. A press-release-and-FAQ habit is associated with Amazon in public writing, but the book and the internal template were not opened in this check, so the steps are not copied. Use the principles page for what Amazon publishes, and mark any PR/FAQ outline you did not read as unknown.
items.tbd: A primary source for the PR/FAQ template that this check can quote.

items.title: Operational requirements
items.summary: The Google SRE book introduction treats running the system as part of the engineering problem. Availability, on-call, and failure communication are requirements when a person depends on the service. Write them with the functional behavior.

items.title: Role names
items.summary: Titles you will see include business analyst, junior or senior business analyst, lead, product owner, and business systems analyst. A title is not a promise of scope. Read the decisions the role owns.

items.title: Levels, without pay
items.summary: A foundation level practices elicitation and clear writing with support. A working level runs a workstream. A senior level sets the analysis approach and coaches others. This lab states no salaries and no 'typical' pay.

items.title: STAR, as a structure
items.summary: Situation, task, action, result is a way to answer a behavioral question without wandering. The result should be something you can point to: a decision, a reduced defect, a baseline. Do not invent a metric for the story.

items.title: Question bank
items.summary: Practice questions: tell us about a stakeholder who disagreed; how you traced a change; how you knew a requirement was testable; how you handled a missing data source. Answer from work you did. Mark practice stories as practice.

items.title: Case interview
items.summary: A case gives you a short brief and too little time. Restate the need, name stakeholders, ask two clarifying questions, then outline scope, risks, and a first model. Say what you are assuming.

items.title: Portfolio pieces
items.summary: Three honest pieces beat a large invented program. A requirement set with acceptance criteria, a process model of a public or personal workflow, and a traceability sample are enough. Remove any private data.

items.title: Resume words
items.summary: Use words you can defend in the interview: elicitation, stakeholder map, user story, acceptance criteria, BPMN, traceability, UAT, workshop. Do not list a tool you have not opened.

items.title: Contracting notes

items.title: Sponsorship
items.summary: Whether an employer will sponsor a work visa is the employer's decision and a legal question. Nothing in this lab promises sponsorship or a visa outcome, and this note is not legal advice. The USCIS H-1B page opened on 16 October 2026. It describes a specialty occupation as work that applies a body of highly specialized knowledge and that normally requires a bachelor's or higher degree in a directly related specialty. The petitioner files the petition. Specialty-occupation petitions need a certified labor condition application. The same page showed fee alerts that were in flux, including a note about litigation, so this lab does not quote a fee as settled.
items.tbd: Which fee applies to a given petition. Read the live USCIS page before anyone files.

foundations.five: Business analysis names a need and a change that has value for a named stakeholder. The public BABOK hub describes a core concept model: change, need, solution, stakeholder, value, and context. A tool name is a solution hypothesis. Write the need in a sentence that still makes sense if the tool changes. Say who decides.
example: A generic clinic wants fewer missed lab results. The need is: patients with an abnormal result hear from the clinic the same day. The phone system is a solution idea, not the need.

Stakeholders: the nurse who calls, the patient, the lab, and the medical director who can approve a new step. Value for the patient is timely news. Value for the clinic is a closed loop. Context includes the hours the lab is open.

ecosystem.five: The same techniques show up in product ownership, project delivery, data work, and change. Shared techniques do not mean shared authority. Ask who decides the need, who decides the date, and who accepts the result. This lab uses the BABOK hub as the core public map and cites neighbors only where a page opened.
ecosystem.exampleTitle: Worked example: three roles, one change
example: A generic retailer wants a clearer return. The analyst writes the need and the acceptance checks. A project manager sequences the work. A product owner orders the backlog.
If one person holds two of those, write that down. Hidden decision rights cause the meeting after the meeting.

babok.five: The public contents list six knowledge areas: planning the analysis, elicitation and collaboration, life cycle management, strategy analysis, requirements analysis and design definition, and solution evaluation. Under them sits a long technique list. Learn the question each technique answers. Verification asks if a requirement is fit to use. Validation asks if it is the right one.
example: A generic warehouse releases a pick screen. Evaluation does not stop at launch. Measure mis-picks, ask pickers where the screen slows them, and recommend a change.
The CBAP page makes the same point in its public sample material: limitation assessment happens when a solution is in use in some form.

requirements.five: A requirement is a usable representation of a need. Give it an identifier, a source, an owner, and a test. A user story names a role, a capability, and an outcome. Given, When, and Then, from the Gherkin reference, turn the outcome into a scenario. Trace the scenario to a test. Untraced text is a rumor.
example: As a returns clerk, I want to see why an item was returned, so that I can offer the right next step.

Given a scanned item with a reason code, when the clerk opens the return, then the reason and the allowed next steps are on screen. Unhappy path: the code is missing, and the clerk must capture it before finishing.

modeling.five: Pick the question before the notation. BPMN is for flow: events, activities, gateways. UML is a family of sketches. An ERD names things and relationships. C4 steps from system context to container, component, and code. Stop at the level the audience can use. Draw the unhappy path.
example: Start: a return arrives. Activity: look up the order. Gateway: is the item within the stated window? Yes path: refund. No path: explain the window and stop.
Both paths have an end. The window length is a business rule beside the drawing, so a policy change does not redraw the map.

agile.five: The 2020 Scrum Guide names three accountabilities and five events, plus the product backlog, sprint backlog, and increment. A kanban board shows flow and limits work in progress. A design sprint is a different sequence: understand, sketch, decide, prototype, test. Do not mix those calendars. Course prices that did not render stay unknown.
example: A generic backlog item is ready when the outcome, the acceptance scenario, and the out-of-scope line are written. It is not ready when it only names a screen.
Planning then chooses a slice that can be inspected at review. The review looks at the increment, not at a slide of intentions.

data.five: A measure needs a question, a formula, a source, and an owner. HEART, from the cited Google Research paper, is a set of user-centered categories, not a benchmark. SQL, as the PostgreSQL tutorial introduces it, filters and groups rows. Process mining reconstructs paths from event logs you are allowed to use. Leave unknown numbers blank.
example: Question: are same-day callbacks happening? Formula: abnormal results called the same calendar day, divided by abnormal results received that day. Source: the call log plus the lab file. Owner: the nurse lead. Act when the rate drops under the line the clinic sets.
This lab does not invent the line. The clinic does.

tools.five: Jira, Confluence, Visio, Miro, Lucid, and Figma are places teams keep work. The decision still lives in a sentence a person can accept. Put the outcome and the test on the ticket. Put the decision, the date, and the owner on the page. A polished board with no limit is still a list.
example: Title: show the return reason. Description: the story and one Given-When-Then. Link: the business need identifier. Status moves to done only when that scenario passes.
The screenshot in the ticket is an illustration. The scenario is the requirement.

ai.five: A model can draft a list, a scenario, or a first drawing. A person checks every fact against a source, marks unknowns, and accepts the text before a stakeholder sees it as a requirement. The handoff from a model to a person, in a contact center or a product flow, is itself a requirement. This lab claims no tool expertise for anyone.
example: A model drafts: refunds are always instant. The policy you were given says refunds over a stated amount need a lead. You strike the word always, attach the policy, and mark the threshold as confirmed.
The fluent sentence was not the requirement. The corrected sentence is.

domains.five: The moves stay the same: need, stakeholder, rule, test. The constraints change. Healthcare interoperability has a public overview in HL7 FHIR. Banking, insurance, retail, telecom, and contact centers add their own rules. If a rule was not on a page this lab opened, it is not stated as fact.
domains.exampleTitle: Worked example: two domains, one move
example: A contact reason and a clinical result both need a source, an owner, and a handoff. In the clinic, you do not guess the record rules. In the contact center, you do not guess the retention rules.
Write the constraint as unknown until someone who owns it confirms it.

product.five: Discovery restates the job before the feature. A business case lists options, including do nothing, and only the costs and benefits you can source. Change work names awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, and reinforcement, the words on the Prosci page. Vendor choice weights the criteria before the demos.
example: Need: same-day notice of abnormal results. Options: do nothing, a checklist on paper, a work-queue screen. Costs you can source: staff time for the paper checklist. Benefits you can source: none yet, so the cell stays blank.
Recommendation: pilot the checklist for two weeks and measure. Unknown is a permitted recommendation.

flows.five: A flow is an ordered sequence, not a project plan. The dot moves when motion is allowed. On a phone, or with reduced motion, it stays still. The order of the steps is the lesson.
example: Prepare, talk, send notes, edit from the reply, then baseline. Skipping the reply makes the notes yours alone.

example: A requirement states a condition. A design describes a solution. Say which reading you intend so a reviewer knows.

careers.five: Show a traced requirement, a confirmed model, and a measure with an owner. Practice STAR with a generic story, never a borrowed biography. Pay is not discussed here. Sponsorship is an employer decision and a legal question. The USCIS H-1B page opened for a high-level description of specialty occupations. It is not advice, and this lab promises no visa.
example: Situation: a generic city clinic had no written rule for abnormal-result calls. Task: you were asked to make the rule testable. Action: you interviewed two nurses, wrote one story and one unhappy path, and traced it to a checklist. Result: the pilot checklist was used for two weeks and the open questions were listed.
That story is invented for practice. It is not Lucky's career and not a claim of employment.

interview.ask: Tell me about a requirement you made testable.
interview.better: Use a generic situation, name the task you owned, the scenario you wrote, and a result you could point at. Leave employers unnamed.
interview.weaker: I always write perfect requirements and the business loved me.

interview.ask: How do you handle a stakeholder who wants a tool, not an outcome?
interview.better: Restate the outcome that would still matter if the tool changed. Write both the request and the need. Ask who decides.
interview.weaker: I put the tool name in the ticket and start building.

triage: A retention rule the lawyer already issued
The callback outcome the sponsor asked to pilot
A second chart that repeats the same number
A rewrite of an unrelated billing engine

interviews.q: Describe a time you traced a need to a test.
interviews.star: Situation: a generic returns desk argued about refunds. Task: make one rule testable. Action: write the story, one Given-When-Then, and a link to the policy paragraph. Result: the unhappy path, a missing reason code, was added before anyone called it done.

interviews.q: Describe a time you stopped a solution from running ahead of the need.
interviews.star: Situation: a generic team wanted a new dashboard. Task: name the decision the chart would change. Action: ask for the question, the source, and the owner. Result: the chart waited until those three existed. No tool was purchased in the story.

interviews.q: Describe a workshop that did not decide.
interviews.star: Situation: the sponsor missed a generic prioritization workshop. Task: keep the team from treating drafts as decisions. Action: label every item draft and send notes the same day. Result: the sponsor confirmed two items and rejected one in writing.
